justice: The street allocates substantial space to motor traffic with multiple wide vehicle lanes, while the pedestrian realm is pushed to the edge and appears secondary.
A separated side path is visible on the right behind the landscaped strip, giving non-motorized users some dedicated space rather than forcing them into the carriageway.
No marked crosswalks, curb ramps, or tactile paving are visible in the scene, so accessibility resources are not clearly distributed for users with different mobility needs.
safety: The roadway is wide, smooth, and clearly marked with centerlines and lane lines, which supports predictable vehicle movement.
There are streetlights along the corridor, which can improve visibility and perceived safety after dark.
The landscaped verge and trees separate the side path from moving traffic, reducing direct pedestrian-vehicle conflict, although the broad road geometry may still encourage higher driving speeds.
livability: The corridor is lined with mature trees, shrubs, and open green space, creating a pleasant environmental setting.
The street appears quiet and low in traffic stress at the moment, which can support a calmer everyday experience.
There are no visible shops, active frontages, seating areas, or public gathering amenities, so the space feels more like a transit corridor than a socially vibrant street.
sustainability: Extensive tree canopy and continuous planting strips provide meaningful green infrastructure and likely improve stormwater absorption and air quality.
The visible side path offers potential support for walking and other non-motorized movement, even though bicycle-specific markings are absent.
The corridor contains a large amount of asphalt dedicated to cars, which lowers overall sustainability compared with a more multimodal street design.
aesthetics: Large mature trees on both sides frame the road and create a strong, coherent landscape character.
Trimmed shrubs, planted medians, and neat curb edges make the street look well maintained and visually ordered.
The open, uncluttered view and gentle road curve create an attractive scenic quality with little visual chaos.
comfort: Dense roadside trees provide substantial shade over the edge spaces, improving thermal comfort in warm weather.
The pavement surface of the road appears smooth and well maintained, which benefits physical comfort for drivers and likely also for users of the side path.
The low apparent traffic volume, abundant greenery, and wide setbacks from development contribute to a calm psychological atmosphere.
walkability: A pedestrian path is visible on the right side behind the planting strip, offering a continuous off-road walking space.
However, the walking route is set far from destinations and there are no visible crossings, signals, or curb ramps, which weakens practical pedestrian connectivity.
The street prioritizes long uninterrupted vehicle movement, and the absence of active building frontage or street-level services reduces walking purpose and attractiveness.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, protected cycle track, or bicycle pavement markings are visible on the roadway.
Cyclists may be forced either to share a relatively fast, wide motor-vehicle carriageway or use the side path, whose cycling designation is unclear.
There is no visible bicycle parking, bike signage, or intersection treatment specifically supporting safe and convenient cycling.
